articles.title: After the emergency
articles.content: THE much-anticipated, and somewhat dreaded, emergency in KP was finally proclaimed by the president on Oct 11. The federal cabinet’s recommendation, the summary of the prime minister’s advice to the president, and the proclamation — all three momentous developments — occurred on the same day. The subsequent actions like taking the chief minister — non-functional but still the elected chief minister of the province — into preventive custody by his subordinate police from within the chief minister’s official residence along with many other senior elected officials; transfer and posting of senior and mid-level Civil Service officials; formation of an advisory council to help the governor in his newly acquired functions; the advisory council’s first meeting and the convening of the meeting of the long-neglected provincial apex committee took place within 48 hours of the proclamation, indicating that the federal government had done its homework in anticipation of the proclamation. Besides debating whether the emergency would be imposed or not, the media had also been speculating about the specific article in Part X ‘Emergency Provisions’ of the Constitution that would be finally invoked. Articles 232 and 234 were the ‘favourites’ on TV talk shows and, in the end, the federal government did not disappoint either group betting on the choice of articles, as the proclamation invoked both Article 232 and 234. It seems that the government was not taking any chances. While Article 232 was apparently favoured because it does not set a limit on the period of emergency, it contains a ‘flaw’ in the federal government’s view, as it does not bar the provincial assembly from functioning during the period of emergency under Article 232. The federal government simultaneously invoked Article 234 apparently to render the provincial assembly non-functional during the emergency and to vest all legislative powers in parliament. Invoking both articles simultaneously appears to be unprecedented, although an emergency has been proclaimed about seven times in Pakistan since the adoption of the 1973 Constitution. This manifests the hard line with which the federal government wants to implement the proclamation of emergency. In most media reports, Article 232 has been frequently referred to as the instrument to proclaim emergency, in contrast to Article 234 that, according to these reports, has been used to proclaim governor’s rule. A plain reading of the Constitution, however, does not bear out this distinction. Both articles concern the proclamation of an emergency, and both give the federal government the option to either exercise executive powers directly in the province or designate the provincial governor to do so on its behalf. Article 234 is invoked either on a report from the provincial governor to the president, or after the two Houses of parliament separately pass a resolution asking the president to proclaim an emergency under Article 234. The president may or may not act based on the governor’s report. Still, if the two Houses pass a resolution to this effect, the president must invoke Article 234. Both articles lay down different requirements for parliamentary approval of the proclamation. Article 232 requires that the proclamation be laid before the two Houses for approval by each within 10 days of the proclamation if the latter has been made by the president on his own (which is the case for the emergency proclaimed on Oct 11), and not based on a resolution passed by the provincial assembly. The federal government easily fulfilled this requirement on Oct 14, despite the fiery speeches and the opposition’s subsequent boycott of the proceedings. Article 232 also provides that the proclamation issued under the article be laid before a joint sitting of the two Houses within 30 days. This formality was also fulfilled. The government might survive constitutional challenges, but can face political risks. Article 234 simply requires that the proclamation issued under the article be laid before a joint sitting of parliament. The proclamation will cease to be valid at the end of two months unless the joint sitting extends the validity by another two months. The joint sitting is authorised to grant up to two extensions of two months each, meaning the proclamation of emergency under this article can continue for a maximum of six months. Given the clear majority of the ruling coalition and the PPP, continuing the proclamation of emergency under this article for six months doesn’t seem to pose a challenge for the federal government. The provincial assembly will become functional after six months, but, as seen in the past, federal governments manage to engineer such a change within the assembly during this period that it doesn’t pose a major challenge to the centre. This is more likely because the provincial government will remain non-functional indefinitely under Article 232. While the federal government may be able to surmount constitutional challenges, it might still face serious political difficulties. Although contrary to the warnings of the non-functional chief minister of KP and other PTI leaders, no serious agitation has been witnessed in the country or even in KP so far, it should cause some discomfort to the federal government that none of the political parties other than those in the ruling coalition has supported the proclamation. Articles 232 and 234 do not restrain the high court’s powers, but a serious judicial challenge appears unlikely. However, the majority of proclamations of emergency challenged in the courts previously could not be sustained. Last but probably not least, the federal government and the security establishment have put their prestige at stake by taking on total responsibility to combat and defeat terrorism in the province. After the proclamation of emergency, there is no longer a provincial government to blame for the rising arc of terrorism. The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.
articles.author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob

articles.title: The real reset
articles.content: IN times like this, we need people who tell hard truths while insisting that the present state of our politics is not permanent. On the one hand, White House aide Stephen Miller says that “we live in a world that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power”, and on the other, philosopher Hannah Arendt says that “out of the barrel of a gun grows the most effective command, resulting in the most instant and perfect obedience. What never can grow out of it is power”. In her 1970 book On Violence, Arendt stresses that violence is not a form of power but its opposite. According to her, power is collective, consensual and relational. By contrast, violence is instrumental and coercive; its strength evaporates the moment the threat is evaded or withdrawn. “Violence can always destroy power,” she concludes. Pakistan’s present rulers seem to follow Thucydides’ thought: “The strong do what they can, and the weak suffer what they must.” Against this backdrop, they want to reset thecollapsed system of governance,according to the minister in charge of internal security and cricket affairs that show clear signs of deterioration. Instead of taking responsibility, he has blamed others for the system’s rot. During his tenure, the security situation in Balochistan and KP has deteriorated significantly. Moreover, widespread violence was witnessed in AJK before the recent polls there. The first move to reset the system was to promulgategovernor’s ruleand proclaim an indefinite emergency in a province where an opposition political party with strong public support had been in power since early 2024. The reasons given are couched in a security narrative. The KP government had failed to control the tide of terrorism since it was at the helm of affairs during the last two to three years. The TTP had unleashed terror in the province, especially in five key border districts on the Afghan border. Many tribal jirgas and multiparty forums held by the provincial legislature opposed the military operations and the use of drone technology that resulted in civilian casualties and population displacement. The protest march led by the chief minister was a political move to persuade the ruling elite to adhere to the Islamabad High Court and Supreme Court decisions to allow access to the incarcerated founder of their party. The SC had directed the prisoner to be treated in a private hospital, in the presence of his physicians and family members. Those court orders were flouted. A simple, humane gesture of following the court’s directions would have defused the political tension between the ruling elite and the opposition parties. Two mainstream parties have lost out the most in the KP fiasco: the PML-N and PPP. The security situation in Balochistan is far more daunting. Why is there no governor’s rule or emergency there? The security situation in Balochistan is far more daunting. There, the state faces an armed insurgency in Baloch-dominated areas. The number of terrorist incidents over the last two years is higher than in KP, and the level of violence against the state agencies, including the police, civil armed forces, and the military, is far more serious than anywhere else. Why is there no governor’s rule or emergency there? The answer is simple: the governing administration there is aligned with the establishment. A security strategy based on force has alienated the Baloch youth from the state. Even the Pakhtun areas close to the Afghan and KP borders are reeling under the onslaught of terrorist organisations that are exploiting internal fissures in the two provinces. Here, we must ask a basic question: what kind of governance structure should dominate Pakistan? Should it be the constitutional order envisioned by the country’s founders, where every citizen is equal under the law, due process is respected, and all institutions act within their legal bounds? Or should Pakistan remain an eternal security state, where justice, lawmaking, foreign policy, the economy, and internal affairs are militarised? A state can justify its power in three ways: by promoting shared values rather than imposing a narrative; by ensuring the sanctity of the electoral process and the rule of law; and by establishing performance legitimacy. The present ruling elite struggles to pass this test. The current governance model needs a reset. Here is how to do it. First, true representation can emerge only through fair and free elections. A state machinery that cannot hold free elections loses credibility and citizens’ trust. Parliament must represent the people’s will. We need a new and independent election commission. Internal stability and cohesion will remain elusive if questions about the legitimacy of the ruling set-up persist. Only a renewed and fair public mandate at this stage can settle these questions. Second, centralised control must be replaced with genuine provincial autonomy and strong local self-government. We must adhere to the letter and spirit of the original 1973 Constitution, as the promise of provincial autonomy was the cornerstone of the near-consensus social contract between the state and society. Third, the independence of the judiciary must be restored by genuine representatives in the new parliament elected through fair mid-term polls. The judiciary’s role in upholding the rule of law and fair administration of justice is crucial to a democratic state. Fourth, our premier federal intelligence agencies appear to be operating outside the legal framework. This lack of accountability must be addressed through parliamentary oversight and laws that clearly define the role of the agencies in both the internal and external security dimensions. Fifth, terrorism and violent extremism should be addressed by faithfully adhering to the updated CT NAP in 2021 through a long-term, sustainable strategy that invests in non-kinetic measures to address these challenges. Short-term kinetic military operations must be followed by multi-stakeholder, whole-of-society engagement strategies and action plans. Finally, a meaningful reset can happen only if the security state does not involve itself in political matters.
articles.author: Tariq Khosa

articles.title: Terror & governance
articles.content: EFFECTIVE governance is the best antidote to terrorism. The state’s counterterrorism response has to showcase its best governance practices, including kinetic and non-kinetic means. Terrorism is like a disease that proliferates when it gets a propitious environment. Public frustrations, lack of livelihood, lax policing, and an administrative vacuum serve as the perfect palette for the spread of terrorism. The merged districts of KP have been affected by a prolonged wave of terrorism, because of which the full range of development and economic initiatives could not be delivered. These areas, wracked by terrorism since the early 2000s, have seen instability due to cross-border movement during the Taliban resistance era of 2003-2021, and an influx of terrorists after 2021. The hurried US withdrawal left Afghanistan in the hands of a Taliban regime with a mediaeval outlook on statecraft as well as interstate relations. Terrorist entities like the TTP that were pushed out from the merged districts through a series of military operations culminating in Operation Zarb-i-Azb, staged a comeback in 2021 after the US departure. Contrary to Pakistan’s expectations, the Afghan Taliban regime’s policy towards the TTP was driven through a mix of considerations, which included ideological kinship, ethnic affinity, internal power struggles, and an instrument to exert leverage on its neighbour. The TTP had internalised a belief which treated the US withdrawal as a great victory for the Afghan Taliban that needed to be replicated in Pakistan. They, therefore, got emboldened and refused to abjure violence. Despite an attempt by the government of Pakistan to co-opt them in the national mainstream, the TTP demanded the reversal of Fata’s merger and a governance structure alien to Pakistan’s Constitution. Misplaced rapprochement with the TTP led to a new wave of terrorism in KP’s merged districts that gradually spread to the settled areas. Terrorist attacks in KP shot up thereafter. Extraordinary times call for extraordinary steps. LEAs in KP required full government support for acting against the TTP terrorists who had started operating from secure sanctuaries in Afghanistan as well as selected spaces within Pakistan’s merged districts. Single-minded focus was required for kinetic CT operations which, however, was missing in a provincial government consumed by agitational politics. Community mobilisation by public representatives was also stymied due to the confrontational stance of the provincial government against the centre. Several measures to improve the development and governance aspects in the merged districts were needed, which were not accorded desired priority. These measures included capacity building of the police, establishment of the judicial infrastructure, strengthening the CTD apparatus, and the economic integration of merged districts into the rest of Pakistan. The National Action Plan was also not fully implemented. The nexus between crime and terrorism remained unchecked. No effort was made to connect the masses in the merged districts with the state through alternative livelihood opportunities after a crackdown on smuggling and the closure of border trade. According to research statistics of an Islamabad-based think tank, 72 per cent of the terrorists killed in CT operations were below 30 years, while 65pc of them were illiterate or primary qualified, and 66pc jobless. In the absence of much-needed synergy between the provincial government and the LEAs, CT efforts remained fragmented and desultory, giving space to terrorists to peddle their na-rrative. A provincial government whose energ- ies were consumed by rhetoric, political wrangling, and agitational marches, could not keep its eye on the ball to fight the difficult battle against terrorism. Without single-minded focus, clarity of objectives and sincerity of purpose, the hydra-headed monster of terrorism cannot be slayed. The Irish example is relevant to KP’s war on terrorism. In Ireland, the conviction rate of terrorists was abysmally low while their mystique was alluring for a population sympathetic to the heroic status of the Irish Republican Army cadres. The British government introduced a package of reforms by building police capacity and picking the best officer, given the title of ‘chief constable’, as a lead terrorism responder, keeping the army in reserve. The judiciary was strengthened through Diplock courts, where the identity of the judges was concealed for their protection. These reforms broke the back of terrorism and the IRA opted for the Good Friday Agreement. Extraordinary times call for extraordinary steps. If a government does not wish to confront the clear and present danger to the life and property of its people, then it should make way for a dispensation capable of undertaking the difficult task abdicated by it.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: Imaginary justice
articles.content: ON any given day, newspaper headlines across Pakistan are littered with updates on court cases. These usually fall into two categories. The first are updates on cases involving political leaders in prison: so and so is brought out for a hearing, so and so has a case stayed. The second category comprises criminal cases that have, largely owing to social media, attracted some attention. Many involve female victims who were killed or raped, sometimes both. Dead women are a topic of interest in Pakistan — much more so than living women. There is, however, a third category of cases. These belong to ordinary people — everyday folk who, often erroneously, imagine that Pakistan’s court system can actually deliver justice. The statistics are alarming. According to the Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan, more than 2.2 million cases were pending in Pakistani courts at the end of December 2025. Most of these are civil cases, and if you are unlucky enough to have to file one, you may wait years, sometimes decades, for a final resolution. An entire generation can be conceived, born and raised before your inheritance dispute with your siblings is resolved. According to one research paper that analysed the backlog, reasons for delays include frequent adjournments, shortages of judicial officers, inadequate process serving, improper working environments, poor record-keeping facilities, and few resources to run the courts. Justice, obviously, is not a priority for Pakistan’s rulers. It is not surprising then that the World Justice Project, which issues an annual report on the rule of law in various countries, ranked Pakistan 130th out of 143 countries in 2025. Pakistan was thus among the 14 lowest-ranked countries for adherence to the rule of law. Accountability, quite obviously, is a fantasy. The situation, and the mental picture of thousands and thousands of files piled high with millions of people awaiting justice, is reminiscent of Charles Dickens’ Bleak House, which tells the story of a case that went on for decades. Portions of the opening paragraph read: “Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.” Fog in Dickens’ narrative stands not simply for the weather phenomenon but also for the murky opacities of a convoluted justice system. More appropriately, a parallel could be drawn with the smog that often settles over Pakistani cities. Smog — a consequence of environmental impurities and societal apathy — has nowhere to go so it suspends itself over human life and can be enumerated in the millions of untended files pushed from hearing to hearing. Sometimes a judge is unavailable, sometimes the lawyers are absent. The emphasis is on everyone except the poor, hapless souls who imagined that justice was a possibility. The smog, of course, is a metaphor, but it points to lived truths about life in Pakistan. If you are an ordinary person, you live a life on the defensive. When you leave your house, you carry only hope and a prayer. If something goes wrong — your parked car gets hit by a passing truck, your phone is stolen, someone attacks you — you realise just how vulnerable you are. No one will replace your car or your phone, and if your attacker can bribe law enforcers with a bigger pile of cash than you can offer to have them file an FIR, then no one will care about that either. Accountability, quite obviously, is a fantasy. All this illustrates how the inability to count on a functioning legal system creates a contor- ted society that functions according to the crudest calculations of power. The inability to obtain justice does not simply impede your ability to recover money owed to you or resolve an inheritance dispute. It also means that in any interaction, calculations are made about who has more power and who has less. If a middle-class person has the misfortune of getting into a dispute with someone very wealthy, it is not law that will determine the outcome; it is power. Solutions like model courts and alternative dispute resolution mechanisms have been thrown at the problem. These have not resolved the underlying structural weaknesses. Pakistan’s courts do not fail simply because there is a need for more courts or another mechanism for resolving disputes. They fail, the argument goes, because powerful Pakistanis — those who draw their power from wealth or brute force — do not believe in the rule of law. The consequence is a legal system that serves as a gloss to disguise the crimes of the powerful while the weak remain cowed and tortured by the failures of a sham system. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: No talks
articles.content: THE opposition Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan hasannouncedthat there will be no more talks with the government till the latter yields on the one thing it has resolutely sought to prevent: a meeting with jailed former prime minister Imran Khan. Having handed authority for further negotiation to Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai, the TTAP has made that meeting a precondition for a return to the table. If there is any desire among the decision-makers to keep political temperatures in check, the government will take up Mr Achakzai’s offer to reason with Imran. The opposition leader is, after all, a veteran politician viewed with respect across party lines. Unfortunately, it is unlikely that the government is in a reflective mood. It not only managed to dismiss the elected PTI government in KP, but has also had its decision approved by a joint sitting of parliament. That move has poisoned the well. The trouble is that few, other than those who imposed emergency andgovernor’s rule on KP, are convinced of the government’s ‘security’ rationale, which they see as a fig leaf for an overreaction by the government and its allies, that is unlikely to hold for long: the set-up imposed on the province faces daunting odds. In the four-and-a-half years since the PTI’s government in the centre was ousted, its successors have failed to deliver better living conditions to the people. The people have only heard the words ‘austerity’ and ‘stabilisation’ during this period, and it has often seemed that the former, in particular, has applied only to the public at large, while those responsible for steering the country out of a protracted polycrisis have merely assigned blame and levelled accusations. Every day that passes adds to the public’s disaffection with the mode of governance. The government should understand that the PTI’s protest march and its reaction to it will look like nothing more than a storm in a teacup on the timescale against which governance is measured. It may not realise it, but it has fallen into the same trap the PTI fell into during its truncated time in power. The PTI remained obsessed with hounding its opponents over corruption; the governments that have followed it have similarly consumed themselves with hounding the PTI out of the political sphere. All seem to be missing the big picture — an economy stretched to its limits and a populace experiencing increasing levels of hunger and poverty while outsized egos clash against each other. It is regrettable that the politics of one of the largest, most populous nations of the world has been reduced to single-item vendettas. This must stop. Mr Achakzai has offered a way back to the table, and the government should seize the opportunity.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Strengthening LGs
articles.content: THE ECP has done well to refuse to allow the Punjab administration to push the local government elections to April. It should now hold its ground. Four years after the last elected councils left office, the province is still looking for reasons not to hold the polls. The reasons, though, keep changing. In August, the provincial authorities agreed to a window between Dec 15 and Jan 15. Two months later, they discovered that the months of December and January are foggy and cold, and that Ramazan would begin in February. None of this is news. Winter arrives every year, and the Ramazan calendar was not a surprise to anyone who signed off on the August consultations. LGs are the tier of the state closest to the people. They handle sanitation, water supply, street lighting, primary health and schooling, and local roads, and generally keep the town running. In functioning democracies, this is where citizens learn to hold someone accountable, and where future political leaders learn to govern. Provincial and federal parties know this, and many are uncomfortable with the fact. An elected mayor with a budget and a mandate is a rival centre of power. A commissioner or deputy commissioner who answers to the chief minister is not. So elections are delayed, laws rewritten whenever the government changes, and administrators fill the space that elected representatives should occupy. The Constitution requires each province to set up an LG system and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility, and authority to its elected representatives. Holding elections is only the first step. Every provincial government, especially Punjab, has treated even that step as optional, and the ones that have held elections have often hollowed out the institutions afterwards. Councils without control over their own funds, staff or functions are decorative. This matters more now than it did before. The debate on improving governance by creating new provinces has gathered pace, and it rests on a sound observation. Provinces are too centralised to serve their citizens from afar. A new provincial map, however, will not help. The new provinces will continue to behave like the old ones, hoarding power and funds at the top. If the aim is better governance, the more direct route is to strengthen the tier that already exists in the Constitution but has never been allowed to work.
articles.author: Editorial
